## Overview

My work asks how individuals and organizations collaborate to solve problems no
single actor can solve alone. Public problems rarely respect organizational
charts or jurisdictional lines, so the people and agencies working on them have
to build relationships across those boundaries, and the structure of those
relationships shapes what gets accomplished. I study how these networks form,
what sustains them, and whether they actually improve outcomes, combining social
network analysis with experimental, longitudinal, and causal inference methods.

This research has been supported by the National Science Foundation, the
National Institutes of Health, the Department of Health and Human Services, the
Federal Transit Administration, and USAID.

## Advice, learning, and performance inside organizations

Who do public employees actually turn to for advice, and does it matter? This
strand examines how informal networks inside schools and public agencies shape
learning, performance, and commitment — often diverging sharply from the formal
structures meant to govern them.

## Interlocal collaboration and regional governance

Local governments face complex problems — transportation, flooding, climate
adaptation, service delivery — that spill across their borders. This work
examines when they choose to collaborate, who they partner with, how those
arrangements are structured and contracted, and whether the resulting networks
perform.

## Network theory, methods, and causal inference

Network data is expensive to collect and network claims are notoriously
difficult to make causally. This strand develops approaches to measuring
structure and asks how network science can support credible inference and
pragmatic intervention.

## Crisis, disaster, and emergency response

Extreme events force organizations that have never worked together to coordinate
under severe time pressure. This research traces how response networks form in
the moment, how information moves through them, and what distinguishes systems
that adapt from those that fail.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" title="Selected publications"}
- Comfort, L. K., Kapucu, N., Ko, K., Menoni, S., & Siciliano, M. D. (2020).
  Crisis Decision-Making on a Global Scale: Transition from Cognition to
  Collective Action Under Threat of COVID-19. *Public Administration Review*,
  80(4), 616–622.
  [doi:10.1111/puar.13252](https://doi.org/10.1111/puar.13252)

- Wukich, C., Hu, Q., & Siciliano, M. D. (2019). Cross-Sector Emergency
  Information Networks on Social Media: Online Bridging and Bonding
  Communication Patterns. *American Review of Public Administration*, 49(7),
  825–839.

- Siciliano, M. D., & Wukich, C. (2017). Network Formation During Disasters:
  Exploring Micro-Level Interorganizational Processes and the Role of National
  Capacity. *International Journal of Public Administration*, 40(6), 490–503.

- Comfort, L. K., Siciliano, M. D., & Okada, A. (2011). Resilience, Entropy, and
  Efficiency in Crisis Management. *Risk, Hazards & Crisis in Public Policy*,
  2(3), 1–25.
:::

## Networks, health, and community wellbeing

Recent collaborative work applies network methods to population health and
environmental equity: how safety practices spread through farmworker crews, how
social ties shape adolescent wellbeing, and how environmental burden
concentrates in particular communities.

- Schultz, K., Ivanich, J. D., Whitesell, N., Siciliano, M. D., & Zacher, T.
